title: Reading caramel by colour and smell
subtitle: How to judge the depth of a dry caramel without relying solely on the thermometer
excerpt: Caramel changes colour from pale straw to deep mahogany as the temperature rises. Each shade corresponds to a different flavour depth. The thermometer gives the number; colour and smell tell you whether the caramel is heading in the right direction and when to stop before it burns.
sourceNotes: Caramelisation temperature and colour progression is well-established in confectionery science. The visual and olfactory cues for judging caramel depth are standard teaching points in professional pastry training.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: target temperature for a medium-deep amber caramel suitable for caramel sauce and caramel tarts

glossaryTerms.definition: The chemical transformation of sucrose (sugar) as it is heated above 160°C. The sugar molecules break down and recombine into hundreds of compounds that produce the golden colour, bittersweet flavour, and characteristic smell of caramel.

content.text: Caramel is sugar that has undergone
. The temperature tells you the precise stage; colour and smell confirm what the thermometer shows and warn you when to act quickly before it burns.
Pale straw (155 to 165°C): the first colour change. Faint nutty smell, barely sweet. Suitable for pralines and very light caramel sauces.
Golden amber (165 to 175°C): the classic caramel colour. A warm, sweet, slightly bitter smell. This is the range for caramel sauce, creme caramel, and tarte tatin.
Deep mahogany (175 to 185°C): strongly bitter, complex, coffee-like smell. For crème brûlée, certain pralines, and bitter caramel sauces that balance a sweet filling.
Acrid smoke (above 185°C): burnt. The caramel has gone past its useful range. Discard and start again; the bitter compounds cannot be corrected by adding cream.

Caramel darkens quickly once it begins to colour. The pan retains heat after the hob is off, so the caramel continues to cook for 10 to 15 seconds after you act. Stop the process slightly before the colour you aim for. For a deep amber sauce, pull the pan when the caramel is golden amber and add the cream immediately, the temperature and residual heat take it to the right depth.

The smell of caramel changes ahead of the colour change. A faint sweetness becomes buttery, then bittersweet, then acrid. If you smell burning before you see it in the pan, it is already too late in a thin pan; in a heavy pan you have a few seconds to act. Trust the smell as the first alarm.
Caramel at this stage is above 160°C. If it touches skin, run cold water over it for at least ten minutes and seek medical care if needed.
